extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in computational humor, NLP, and data-science interested in automatic humor detection for cartoon captions
extracted.subtask_description: Automatic classification/identification of funnier captions for single-panel cartoons (e.g., New Yorker Caption Contest) using linguistic, semantic, and surprisal-based features. The goal is to rank or select captions that humans judge as funnier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption length / short and tight
rubrics_metrics.description: Caption length: short captions tend to be funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise, tightly worded captions; avoid verbosity. Corresponds to the rubric question: 'Is the caption short and tight?' Shortness is positively correlated with funniness in their data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word frequency (rarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Word frequency: less common words can be funnier (or more pretentious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using relatively rare or unexpected lexical items can increase humor, but rare words may also come off as pretentious — balance novelty with accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concreteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Concreteness: more concrete words often funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concrete, imageable wording over abstract phrasing to increase humorous impact and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perplexity / negative log-likelihood (surprisingness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative log-likelihood under a language model: surprisingness predicts humor. Funnier captions often have unexpected words at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High surprisal (low probability under an LM) at the punch position is a positive signal. Operationalize with LM perplexity or token-level surprisal, especially near the caption's end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic distance from the scene / avoid describing the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance from the scene: captions semantically distant from what the cartoon literally depicts (less descriptive) tend to be funnier. The caption should not just describe what's already obvious in the cartoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid captions that merely restate the visible content; introduce an interpretation, angle, or unrelated semantic content to create humor. This corresponds to the rubric item: 'Does it avoid simply describing the scene?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment (tone matching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive sentiment captions can be funnier in some contexts; negative sentiment can work for darker cartoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cartoon tone when choosing sentiment; there is no single best polarity — match sentiment to the scene and desired comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification / clearly characterized speaker voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions in first person (a character speaking) often funnier. Specific, named, characterized speakers are better than vague voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a distinct speaker voice or character perspective (first person) to increase humor. This reflects the rubric question: 'Does a clearly characterized speaker voice the line?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity / domain-mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing terms from different domains (incongruity-based features). Domain-mixing predicts humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create unexpected combinations or frame content via cross-domain references (e.g., mixing technical and domestic domains). Incongruity is a key mechanism for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric question: Is the caption short and tight?
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit rubric item asking whether the caption is concise and tightly written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a binary/graded evaluation point: brevity and tight wording are desirable; may be operationalized by character/word count thresholds or by penalizing filler language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric question: Does it avoid simply describing the scene?
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit rubric item asking whether the caption introduces something beyond literal description of the cartoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captions that merely describe the image are weaker; stronger captions add interpretation, surprise, or a twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric question: Are domains mixed (incongruity)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit rubric item asking whether the caption mixes domains to create incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for cross-domain mappings or unexpected associations; domain-mixing is predictive of funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric question: Is the language surprising at the punch position?
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit rubric item focusing on surprisal at the punchline (end) of the caption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an unexpected token or phrase appears at the position that serves as the punch; measureable by LM surprisal or judged by human readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric question: Does a clearly characterized speaker voice the line?
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit rubric item asking whether the line is voiced by a distinct, characterized speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for first-person framing, named roles, or distinctive voice; captions voiced by a clear persona tend to be funnier.
